analysis.title: AI quick pulse: Blue wave, red light for data centers?
key_insights: Democrats took both chambers of Congress in the US midterms and flipped the governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas. Investors sold semiconductor and hardware stocks on the risk of data-center delays and moratoria.

About 346 GW of US data-center capacity is under construction or planned (dcmap.us). Newly Democratic-led states have significant influence over roughly 40% of planned capacity additions, with Texas and Georgia together about 30%.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a data-center moratorium, ending tax incentives and limits on energy and water use. Outgoing Governor Abbott ordered a review of projects before grid interconnection in August 2026 and halted environmental and operational permits in September 2026.

UBS expects the Texas pause to last until the legislature enacts new guidance. With roughly six months left before construction must begin for 2028 deployment, further delays could push some capacity into 2029.
Georgia Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms campaigned on pausing new data-center construction and said she would sign an executive order on taking office, while reviewing tax incentives.

UBS thinks already-approved projects are unlikely to be stopped. About 30 GW in states shifting to Democratic governors should be built over the next 18 to 24 months, limiting near-term disruption to the semiconductor supply chain.
UBS expects capacity shelved by moratoria to relocate to friendlier states rather than disappear, providing a home for chips two to three years out.

Hyperscalers and developers are likely to expand community commitments such as grid upgrades, lower water use, workforce support and transparency. UBS sees costs incrementally higher but not materially so.
Delays should raise the value and pricing power of existing capacity while AI compute demand exceeds supply.

UBS sees execution bumps and volatility across the AI complex. Shipment delays could cause inventory digestion and price cuts, weighing on semiconductor and hardware bottleneck stocks that gained pricing power in recent months.
The likely outcome is a modestly lower growth trajectory with pockets of inventory air gaps, but a lower risk of significant oversupply.
UBS favors hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, Google). If 2028 capex expectations are cut, their free cash flow should improve.
UBS also likes Visa and Mastercard as defensive tech, and Apple and Sony as potential beneficiaries of relief in memory pricing.
Within AI picks and shovels, UBS stays selective and prefers quality names that have not had large margin expansion from recent price increases, since they have less downside if pricing reverses.
CIO no longer rates equities in the Most Preferred, Bellwether and Least Preferred framework or publishes top picks, effective 1 November 2026. It uses a CIO Selected designation instead.

tension_points.bull_case: Approved projects get built, capacity relocates to friendlier states, and delays raise the value and pricing power of existing hyperscaler capacity. Lower 2028 capex would improve hyperscaler free cash flow.
tension_points.bear_case: Moratoria in Texas and Georgia could delay shipments, causing inventory digestion and price cuts for AI semiconductor and hardware stocks, and push some capacity into 2029.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Texas extends its pause until the legislature passes new rules, which could push capacity from 2028 into 2029, with about six months left before construction must begin.
